[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] • Agentic Misalignment (Lynch et al., 2025): tests how readily the model, instantiated as an agent, engages in harmful actions that serve its objective or protect it from being replaced or shut down.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] As reported in our model behavior assessment for Muse Spark 1.1, the model robustly maintains its epistemic integrity, achieving 95.7% honesty score on MASK, and it shows a low tendency toward self-preservation under pressure, getting a 1.1% harmful action rate across all tasks on Agentic Misalignment (Section 1.1.3).
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] We detected high rates of verbalized evaluation awareness for Agentic Misalignment ( 79%), along with statistical significant performance differences between rollouts where awareness is verbalized and those where it is not.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Agentic Misalignment.
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] The Agentic Misalignment benchmark (Lynch et al., 2025) tests whether models, instantiated as an email-oversight agent in a simulated corporate environment, will take harmful actions (across blackmail, corporate espionage, and lethal-action scenarios) when these are the only available means to preserve their goals or avoid being replaced.

[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] Of the four alignment evaluations in this analysis, one shows a statistically significant difference between aware and unaware rollouts: Agentic Misalignment (p < 0.001), where evaluationaware rollouts are less harmful (harmfulness rate 0.3% vs. 4.1%).
[meta-muse-spark-1-1-system-card] The probe is entirely post-hoc: we reuse the trajectories from the agentic misalignment and MASK evaluations reported above and split them, by each evaluation’s own scoring, into trajectories where the model misbehaved and trajectories where it did not.
